Headline: Gamma-TiAl may have a hot-salt stress-corrosion-cracking (HSSCC) onset temperature below the ~260-290 C "floor" assumed from the 1962-72 Ti-alloy corpus, because the alumina scale that Ondrejcin (NASA CR-1133, 1968) identified as a catalytic accelerator of NaCl pyrohydrolysis is the native scale of a 48 at% Al aluminide from t=0, maximising the HCl source term the mechanism needs.
Old source: Ondrejcin, R. S., and Louthan, M. R. Jr., "Role of Hydrogen Chloride in Hot-Salt Stress Corrosion Cracking of Titanium-Aluminum Alloys," NASA CR-1133 (also DP(NASA)-1130), E. I. du Pont de Nemours & Co., Savannah River Laboratory, August 1968. https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19680023547/downloads/19680023547.pdf — body, selective-attack table (Table II: oxide/metal Al ratios 2-3x on Ti-Al alloys), and p.17 "aluminium oxide acts as an accelerator in the pyrohydrolysis of difficultly hydrolyzable salts such as NaCl." Accelerator claim cites Kirk-Othmer Encyclopedia of Chemical Technology v.14 p.215 (1955) and Rodden ed., Analytical Chemistry of the Manhattan Project p.729 (McGraw-Hill 1950) — neither retrieved; this is the lead's weakest joint.
Modern problem: Modern HSSCC literature (including Dye-group work, e.g. arXiv:2009.10567 and D2-18O crack-tip experiments at 450 C) inherits Ondrejcin's conclusion (susceptibility rises with Al; Al is preferentially attacked) while dropping his accelerator mechanism. The 1962-72 stressed test matrix capped at ~8 wt% Al (Ti-8Al-1Mo-1V the high-Al extreme); the TiAl-era literature uses an unstressed superalloy hot-corrosion protocol at 700-900 C. No source puts stressed bulk gamma-TiAl under solid NaCl in 300-500 C. The two literatures describe the same quantity (Al2O3 at a chloride interface) with opposite valence, and nothing forces them to meet.
Cheapest next check: Two paper + bench steps BEFORE any SCC rig. (a) Interlibrary-loan Kirk-Othmer 1955 v.14 p.215 and Rodden 1950 p.729; verify whether either names Al2O3 (vs U3O8/WO3/V2O5) as a pyrohydrolysis accelerator. ~$0-40, 3-10 days. (b) HCl-evolution screen on 0.1 mg/cm2 solid NaCl over (i) alpha-Al2O3 powder, (ii) TiO2 powder, (iii) 50/50 mix, (iv) scraped Ti-48Al-2Cr-2Nb scale, (v) blank — isothermal holds at 400/350/300/250/200 C in moist air, chloride by IC on NaOH-trapped effluent. ~$4-8k, 2-3 weeks. Only if alumina raises chloride yield over TiO2 in 250-350 C should the stress ladder be built.
Verifier notes: Verifiers in the upstream ledger independently fetched both primary copies of CR-1133 (NTRS and sti.srs.gov DP(NASA)-1130), extracted the text locally, and confirmed the accelerator sentence verbatim on p.17, along with Table II's Al enrichment numbers (28.6/7.7, 7.8/5.9, 13.9/5.2, 11.6/4.3), the V/Sn-depletion statement that makes the enrichment Al-specific, and the NaOH-strips-Al mitigation control. One verifier scored 7 and called this "the strongest-sourced lead I have checked in this series." The author line and report numbers were read directly from the SRS title page, not reconstructed from a metadata aggregator. Where the lead is exposed is not citation fidelity but the depth of the citation chain beneath Ondrejcin's own accelerator sentence: it rests on a 1955 handbook cite with no measurement, and the modern pyrohydrolysis-accelerator literature names WO3, U3O8 and Cr2O3 while treating alumina as the matrix, never the catalyst. The bridge also quietly converts "composition of a reactively-grown corrosion product" into "Al2O3 activity in the protective scale", which are different physical objects. The one upstream verifier who voted refuted (score 3) argued: CR-1133 Table III reports a Ti-8Al-1Mo-1V hot-salt crack threshold temperature of 232 C — on the alloy with the 28.6 wt% Al corrosion product, i.e. the maximum-scale-alumina case in the 1962-72 matrix. A ~4x spread in scale Al across that series moved severity and threshold stress, never onset temperature; lower-Al Ti-6Al-4V has a reported field failure at 220 C (wrong sign); and at 300-500 C a TiAl scale is a thin transient mixed TiO2/Al2O3 film, not protective alpha-alumina — so interfacial alumina activity may be far lower than the bulk composition suggests. The two paper + bench steps above are designed to settle the catalytic-rationale half directly before anyone commits to an SCC rig. Caveats carried from the upstream verifiers: - The Cranfield PhD thesis "Elevated Temperature Oxidation and Corrosion of a Titanium Aluminide Alloy" (handle 1826/3584) is the closest grey-literature threat. Indirect reporting indicates air/SO2 kinetics at or above 800 C (not NaCl, not stressed, not the lead's window), but the document itself could not be opened (HTTP 403) and should be pulled from the Cranfield repository before anyone commits to the stress ladder. - Yao & Marek (1995) found no NaCl-induced corrosion of TiAl in oxygen-free exposure, so the route needs oxygen/moisture — consistent with pyrohydrolysis. - Dye's group argues oxygen (not hydrogen) from water vapour is the main embrittling species at 450 C, which would partly decouple cracking severity from the HCl source term this lead keys on. - ONERA's US 8,617,323 B2 already treats salt-exposed TiAl parts as needing protection and describes an AlCl3 → HCl → re-attack loop; the chemistry is not virgin ground even if the stressed threshold question is. Score 7/5/3 (one of three verifiers voted refuted) in the upstream ledger entry of 2026-10-21. Upstream destination: undecided. Found by an automated literature sweep; not refereed. A hypothesis worth one cheap check, not a finding.

Headline: Wiederhorn & Bolz (1970) Table II already contains composition-resolved subcritical-crack-growth parameters (E*, b, ln v0) for a low-alkali aluminosilicate and a 7740-type borosilicate — the two families now used as glass package cores — together with a closed-form time-to-failure integral; the glass-core packaging literature (McCann 2017 → Micromachines 2025) cites this same corpus only for the water-reduced fracture energy (8 → 1.98 J/m^2), using the static threshold while discarding the kinetics printed in the same papers.
Old source: Wiederhorn, S. M., and Bolz, L. H., "Stress Corrosion and Static Fatigue of Glass," J. Am. Ceram. Soc. 53(10) 543-548 (October 1970), NBS. DOI 10.1111/j.1151-2916.1970.tb15962.x. Scanned text: https://belglas.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/10/wiederhorn_stress_corrosion.pdf — Table II: Aluminosilicate I (Na2O 0.01 wt frac, SiO2 0.57, Al2O3 0.20, MgO 0.12, CaO 0.06) E* 29.0 kcal/mol, b 0.138, ln v0 5.5; Borosilicate (SiO2 0.80, B2O3 0.14) E* 30.8, b 0.200, ln v0 3.5; equivalent power-law n ~22 and ~32 at K_I = 4e5 N/m^1.5, 298 K. Universal-fatigue-curve recipe at Eqs. 3-5. Threshold observed in soda-lime and borosilicate; "no indication of a static fatigue limit" over the measured range in aluminosilicate and silica (an unmeasured absence, not a proven no-threshold).
Modern problem: Le, Yoo & Choa, Micromachines 16(11):1256 (2025) carries G_c = 1.98 J/m^2 in water vs 8 J/m^2 in air as a propagation threshold with zero kinetics, zero Weibull, zero fatigue vocabulary, and reports 99-139 MPa tensile RDL interface stress and ~315 MPa at an edge-crack tip — inside region I. McCann's 2017 Georgia Tech PhD cites W&B as ref [86] but uses only the static G_c; the Corning TGV packaging papers (Shorey/Lu/Smith IMAPS 2015) and the IEEE EPS 2025 AGC glass-core document carry no instance of fatigue, Weibull, proof test or lifetime. Same company carries the full apparatus in its foldable-display patents (US 9,898,046 and siblings) and nothing from it in its packaging papers.
Cheapest next check: ZERO-LAB PRECURSOR (hours, $0): compute the Eq. 4 / Eq. 5 lifetime band for sigma/sigma_N = 0.1-0.2 using b = 0.138 (alkali-free) and b = 0.200 (borosilicate), report alongside power-law equivalent at n_eq ~22 and ~32, and show the spread. If exponential and power-law bounds bracket 10 years from opposite sides, that spread is itself the publishable result. MEASUREMENT (2-3 weeks, ~$10-30k outsourced, near-free inside Corning/Schott/AGC/GT-PRC): ASTM C1368 constant-stress-rate ring-on-ring on existing TGV coupons (AF32 or Eagle XG plus Borofloat 33), 4-5 stress rates spanning 4 decades, ~30 coupons per rate, in 25 C / 50% RH, plus a liquid-nitrogen inert-strength reference. n from the loading-rate slope (1/(n+1), not n). If measured n ~22, the 1970 parameter set transfers.
Verifier notes: The upstream ledger entry survived its three verifiers with no refuted votes (scores 8/5/5). All three fetched Wiederhorn & Bolz (one via r.jina.ai after finding the belglas scan was CCITT image-only, one by parsing the PDF content streams directly) and confirmed Table II's 18 values with standard deviations, Eqs. 1-5, the distilled-water 2-90 C methods, the static-fatigue-limit asymmetry statement, and the abstract's "Sodium was detrimental to stress corrosion resistance." A sibling entry (upstream score 8/3/7, same date) argues the same bridge from the threshold-asymmetry angle — that for a permanently loaded part a threshold is the only thing that buys unbounded life, and the alkali-free chemistries selected for glass cores are the two in which W&B observed no threshold over their measured range. Both entries recommend the same dynamic-fatigue measurement; this lead merges them. Caveats the upstream verifiers raised, carried verbatim: 1. **The form is exponential (Charles-Hillig), not the power law v = A K^n the modern packaging literature uses.** NASA's own TM-103543 states that at a proof ratio of 3.0 the two forms differ by a factor of ~60 in predicted life for soda-lime — the output is model-form-sensitive before it is n-sensitive. The deliverable is a bound family, not a lifetime number. 2. **"Aluminosilicate I" is low-alkali (Na2O 0.01 wt fraction), NOT alkali-free, and is a 1723-type glass, not AF32 or Eagle XG.** The paper's own headline finding is that sodium content dominates stress-corrosion resistance, which is the axis a substitution needs to clear. 3. **W&B themselves state the universal-fatigue-curve equation "does not describe stress corrosion phenomena for very short failure times or for failure times approaching the fatigue limit"**, and that the curves are valid only to log t ~ 3.5. A glass-core 10-year service life is exactly the long-duration extrapolation they disclaim. 4. **The no-threshold result for aluminosilicate is an absence of evidence** the authors explicitly disown ("although one presumably exists for aluminosilicate and silica glasses at lower stress intensity values"). The sharpened claim is "the no-growth stress is unmeasured for this chemistry," not "alkali-free glass has no threshold." Grutzik et al. 2022 and later work partly fill the threshold question in for silica; the alkali-free aluminosilicate chemistries of AF32/Eagle XG remain unmeasured at 25 C. 5. **The measured and calculated characteristic durations do not agree quantitatively in the source itself** (Section IV.3): the experimental slope is ~3x the calculated one, attributed to real abrasion flaws being irregular. This is directly relevant to a laser-ablated plus HF-etched TGV sidewall and is the citation for why a single predicted lifetime would be unjustified. 6. **The claim that the connection is "wholly unmade" was damaged by one verifier**: McCann's 2017 Georgia Tech dissertation does cite W&B 1970 (as [86]) along with Charles's two Static Fatigue of Glass papers, Gy 2003, Ciccotti 2009 and Glaesemann's fibre-reliability method, and reproduces a v-vs-K_I figure. What survives is narrower: packaging stops at a moisture-reduced snapshot threshold and does not integrate v(K_I) forward to a service-life bound, and a region-0 threshold for the specific alkali-free aluminosilicate core chemistries at 25 C does appear unmeasured. 7. **Correction to upstream numbers**: Aluminosilicate I's b is 0.138 (not 0.144); the paper names fused silica as the most stress-corrosion-resistant glass, not aluminosilicate, and groups Aluminosilicate I with borosilicate as intermediate. The counterintuitive direction survives in narrower form. Upstream destination: undecided. Score 8/5/5 (0 refuted) for the Table II / lifetime-bound framing; a sibling entry on the threshold-asymmetry framing scored 8/3/7 (1 refuted) on the same date and is folded into this lead. Found by an automated literature sweep; not refereed. A hypothesis worth one cheap check, not a finding.

Headline: Kansas Experiment Station Bulletin 273 (Hallsted & Mathews 1936) and companion USDA Division of Dry-Land Agriculture publications print year-by-year, station-by-station plant-available soil water in the profile at wheat seeding time for Hays, Colby and Garden City across the onset of the Dust Bowl, measured gravimetrically to 6 ft; these station records have apparently never been used to evaluate any 1930s model soil moisture reconstruction (e.g. Wang et al. 2009, J. Climate, six-LSM ensemble 1920-2003) at the matching grid cells.
Old source: Hallsted, A. L., and Mathews, O. R. (1936), "Soil Moisture and Winter Wheat with Suggestions on Abandonment," Kansas Agricultural Experiment Station Bulletin 273, Manhattan, Kansas, 46 pp. https://extension.k-state.edu/historicpublications/pubs/SB273.pdf — four-cores-per-foot-section to 6 ft, oven-dried, with per-foot minimum points of exhaustion printed (12.1/15.4/13.4/13.4/13.4/15.1 % at Hays). Tables II, III, V, VII give inches of available water at seeding time per year, 1909/1910-1934. SB273 is a seeding-time snapshot ending in 1934. Depth-resolved companions covering 1935-1940 exist and should be read with it: Cole & Mathews, USDA Circular 563 (1940), 15 Great Plains stations 1907-1938; Rogler, G. A., and Haas, H. J. (1947), "Range Production as Related to Soil Moisture and Precipitation on the Northern Great Plains," Agronomy Journal 39(5), Mandan ND, measured fall moisture to 3 and 6 ft, record from 1915.
Modern problem: Wang, H., Schubert, S., Suarez, M., Chen, J., Hoerling, M., Kumar, A., and Pegion, P. (2009), "Attribution of the Seasonality and Regionality in Climate Trends over the United States during 1950-2000," J. Climate 22, and the Andreadis et al. 2005 VIC single-model 1920-2003 reconstruction, both grid-cell soil moisture products. The reanalysis-era Dust Bowl work (e.g. Bolles et al. 2019) reaches NARA Record Group 114 for dust-storm data sheets and still takes soil moisture from 20th Century Reanalysis rather than from any measured station record. Measured soil moisture at these stations has not been published alongside, or regressed against, the modern reconstructions at the matching grid cells.
Cheapest next check: STAGE 0 (free, 30 min): drop "continuously measured" and "1906-1940" from the framing — SB273 is a seeding-time annual snapshot ending 1934. STAGE 1 (~3-4 h, $0): hand-transcribe SB273 Table III only (inches of available water in top 6 ft of the Hays fallow plot, by crop year, ~25 rows) — the K-State scan has usable OCR of the prose but the numeric tables are page images. STAGE 2 (~1 day, $0): pull the Hays grid cell from Wang et al. 2009 (or Andreadis et al. 2005 VIC) and 20CRv3 for Sep-Oct 1910-1934, rank 25 autumns by model soil moisture and by printed inches-of-available-water, compute Spearman rho and Kendall tau on the driest tercile. Pre-register the one result that matters: does the model place autumn 1933 and 1934 at the same rank positions the bulletin does? KILL CRITERION: if Spearman rho is indistinguishable from zero AND 1933/1934 are not co-ranked, stop; do not transcribe other tables or pursue archival leads.
Verifier notes: Upstream verifiers independently fetched the K-State PDF and ran pdftotext (118,712 bytes), confirming the author line, title page, four-core six-foot method, per-foot minimum points of exhaustion verbatim, the 7.7-inch fallow 25-year mean, the r = 0.271 (PE 0.130) within-station correlation, the 1934 "at least 8 feet" passage, and the authors' own refusal to print bulk densities ("Details of the procedure are not important."). AGRIS independently corroborates the citation. The upstream verdict is "worth one cheap check, with the framing narrowed first." Three important corrections from the verifiers must travel with any writeup: 1. **The source is NOT a continuous 1906-1940 series** as any over-eager framing might imply. The bulletin states "only those made at seeding time are considered here," and no 4-digit year later than 1934 appears in the text. It is an annual autumn snapshot covering only the drought's onset. 2. **"The only such numbers in print" is false.** Rogler & Haas 1947 (Agron. J. 39(5), Mandan ND, fall moisture to 3 and 6 ft, station record from 1915) covers 1935-1940, which SB273 lacks. Cole & Mathews USDA Circular 563 (1940) prints similar foot-section available-water determinations for 15 Great Plains stations 1907-1938. SSSAJ 18:247-252 (1954) publishes the USDA Dry-Land programme's soil-moisture data for 31 Great Plains locations and includes the per-depth field-capacity and minimum-point calibration that SB273 declines to give. Any publishable work should use these as the broader denominator, not SB273 alone. 3. **Plot-scale fallow records are not landscape.** Fallow storage efficiency is itself drought-dependent; the bulletin's own fallow-water-to-yield correlation is "a very low degree of relationship" (r = 0.271). Grid-cell comparison must treat printed plots as a bracket on the range, not a point estimate. The upstream refuting verifier (score 3) argued these corrections kill the uniqueness claim; the lead survives in narrower form — the measurements are real, cold, printed, overlap the 1930s, and are uncited by the modern soil-moisture-reconstruction literature. The right output is a published Spearman rho on a pre-registered pair of years, not a reconstruction. Upstream score 6/6/3 (one refuted) on 2026-10-21; destination undecided. Found by an automated literature sweep; not refereed. A hypothesis worth one cheap check, not a finding.

Headline: Landauer's 1954-56 Site 2 Greenland excavation experiment measured non-hydrostatic firn deformation in natural névé at the exact site whose 1-D depth-density profile underpins the canonical compressibility parameter k ~ 1000 of GM97-based firn models — four geometries, four tunnel diameters at eight stations, two trenches and a 30.5 m deep pit, with closure rates already tabulated as strain rates — and these field data have never entered modern firn rheology.
Old source: Landauer, J. K. (1957), "On the deformation of excavations in the Greenland névé," U.S. Army Snow, Ice and Permafrost Research Establishment (SIPRE), Research Report 30, April 1957, 14 pp. + appendix. Also IUGG/IASH Toronto 1957, vol. 4, 475-491. Handle: https://hdl.handle.net/11681/2693 (ERDC DSpace OCR text via the REST-API path /server/api/core/bitstreams/.../content). Site 2, -24.4 C below 10 m, accumulation 41.5 g/cm2/yr, "melting ... is a very infrequent phenomenon." Tables I-VII: tunnel closure strain rates on four diameters at eight stations, trench reaches, deep-pit closure at seven levels, vertical-strain rates in 13 layer intervals, depth/density/overburden/experimental m/calculated viscosity to 40 m, and in-tunnel density profile against undisturbed background. Landauer rejects Nye's incompressible solution and derives sigma_z/sigma_y = m-1 (m = viscous/plastic analogue of 1/Poisson's ratio).
Modern problem: Jog. 2025.6 (DOI 10.1017/jog.2025.6) fixes k against 1-D depth-density at six Greenlandic sites, Site 2 among them (its Fig. 4), and concedes it has only one deviatoric experiment — a warm-year NEEM tunnel — and that no single calibration is applicable to all six cores. Landauer, Mellor and SIPRE appear zero times in that paper's references. Grinsted et al. 2026 (egusphere-2026-3464) reports viscous Poisson ratios systematically lower than the Zwinger reference and "pronounced non-monotonic" in density, and states a and b are "ill-posed" from one site; same zero occurrence of Landauer/Mellor/CRREL deformation reports. The connection to Landauer's cold multi-geometry Site-2 dataset has not been made.
Cheapest next check: 1-2 days of one glaciologist-modeller's time, no new data, no cost. Reframe FIRST: do NOT invert Landauer's raw vertical/oblique/horizontal ratio for k — his own Discussion attributes that ratio to the overburden viscosity gradient and the free surface, not to compressibility, and verifier algebra shows the measured 3.3x anisotropy sits outside the admissible range for every compressibility in his model. INSTEAD invert the oblique diameters (the only pair his own theory already reproduces: 9 theoretical vs 10 observed, x1e-10 s^-1) and use the vertical:horizontal contrast only as a sign/consistency test. From the saved OCR take Table I stations WE/WF1/WF2 and Table IV levels 3.1-29 m; pair each strain rate with Landauer's measured density and calculated sigma_z (discard the m and eta columns — they are lab-imported from SIPRE Report 7). Run the 2025 paper's own Elmer/Ice GM97 setup repointed to Site 2 at k = 300, 1000, 3000 with a depth-resolved viscosity field. Pass/fail: if no k in 300-3000 reproduces both the oblique rate and the pit's weak depth dependence (4.3 cm/yr at 3.1 m to 1.8 cm/yr at 29 m), that is a publishable negative result about GM97's near-surface compressibility.
Verifier notes: All three upstream verifiers survived their refutation attempts (scores 7/6/5, 0 of 3 refuted). They independently fetched RR 30 (ungated via the ERDC DSpace REST path, since the HTML interface is CAPTCHA-gated and DTIC was down), extracted 29.8 kB of OCR, and verified Table I at station WE (22.2 / 7.8 / 7.8 / -0.7 cm/yr with strain rates 0.11 / 0.033 / 0.033 / -0.0027 yr^-1), Table VII's Site 2 parameters, the -24.4 C / 41.5 g/cm2-yr site conditions, the explicit rejection of Nye's incompressible solution, and the m = 2 hydrostatic remark — all verbatim. The author line was taken from the DSpace item record AND the document's own title page. The modern end was also verified: jog.2025.6 states k = k_a = k_b ~1000 as canonical, its Fig. 4 is "Modeled Site 2 density profiles for various k", it concedes low confidence in the NEEM validation and that "no single calibration is applicable to all six cores", and neither Landauer nor Mellor appears in its reference list. Caveats carried from the verifiers, in strict form: 1. **The naive three-way-ratio inversion the first draft proposed does not work.** Landauer's Eq. 12 angular factor gives a vertical/oblique ratio bounded on (1, 1.657]; the measured ratio is 3.3-3.5, outside the admissible range for every compressibility, and the horizontal/oblique prediction is strictly positive while the measurement is negative. Landauer himself attributes the anisotropy to a 40x viscosity gradient across the overburden, not to compressibility. The reframed check (oblique diameters + deep-pit depth-dependence against a depth-resolved viscosity field) survives, which is the version above. 2. **Table VII's m(z) column is imported from SIPRE Report 7 lab tests, not measured by this field experiment.** The "field-anchored Poisson curve" framing is incorrect; what is field-measured are the strain rates, densities and calculated overburden stresses. 3. **Landauer's own theory under-predicts the field closure substantially** (theoretical vs observed radial strain rates 14 vs 35 x1e-10 s^-1 vertically, 2 vs -0.9 horizontally; deep-pit observed rates 1.5-2.6x the calculated ones). He attributes this to using viscosity at the tunnel centre when the softer overlying firn controls roof descent; the same direction (real firn softer under deviatoric load than Sorge-law viscosity implies) is why the 2025 paper needed a large k. 4. **Landauer assumes a linear Newtonian flow law; GM97 uses n = 3.** His fitted parameters cannot be transplanted; only his raw closure/strain-rate data can be re-inverted. 5. **Bender 1967 (Sapporo Physics of Snow and Ice proceedings) re-tested the same inversion on the same tunnel after 11 years and reported failure, with the same failure at Wilkes (Cameron 1961) and South Pole (Ramseier 1962).** Any writeup should anchor on Bender rather than Landauer, and should include a vertical-only background densification correction (worth 15-25% of the vertical closure per Bender). 6. **The "corpus-unreachable" story is softer than first claimed.** The 2025 paper does cite CRREL TR 174 (Clark 1965, Camp Century) and the 2026 preprint cites CRREL RR 220, Bader, Salm and Shinojima — the group is fluent in this literature and simply prefers lab calibration. Landauer RR 30 was one catalogue step away and was still missed; that is what makes it a hypothesis worth one cheap check. 7. **The lead's 6 m, rho ~0.45 target regime is exactly where the group itself says GM97's n = 3 breaks down**, so a k fitted there would absorb a constitutive-form error. The check must use the authors' own published FEniCS repo on Landauer's Site 2 geometry with a pre-declared kill criterion. 8. **Gate the follow-up on initial-condition data**: whether a record of the 1954 excavation and backfill state survives. If not, drop it. Upstream score 7/6/5 (0 refuted) on 2026-10-21; destination undecided. Found by an automated literature sweep; not refereed. A hypothesis worth one cheap check, not a finding.

Headline: Wittig (2017) derived from 67 systematically surveyed Lusatian lignite-dump static-liquefaction events a dimensionless arrest criterion — the toe-to-crest groundwater-depth ratio h_F/h_K must exceed about 0.333 for horizontal flow to be prevented — in which slope angle and unit weight drop out of the expression entirely; this criterion, and the ~125-event Lusatian event population behind it, has not reached the tailings-flow-mobility literature where Ghahramani et al. 2020 (NHESS) explicitly tried and failed to stratify a 33-event area-volume regression by flow-path confinement.
Old source: Wittig, Manfred (2017), "Geokinematische Ablaeufe bei der Verfluessigung von Tagebaukippen," in 18. Geokinematischer Tag, Freiberg 2017, pp. 102-123, TU Bergakademie Freiberg / Institut fuer Markscheidewesen und Geodaesie. https://tubaf.qucosa.de/api/qucosa%3A23146/attachment/ATT-0/ — Si = (K_p h_F^2) / (K_a h_K^2); for phi = 30 degrees, h_F/h_K > 0.333 (0.394 at FOS 1.4); validation on 67 Weissbach & Kudla (2014) events gives 5 category-3 (local collapses), 43 category-2 (vertical equilibrium only), 19 category-1 (full Setzungsfliessen). Companion: Weissbach & Kudla (2014), 67-event compilation, TU Bergakademie Freiberg Institut fuer Bergbau und Spezialtiefbau; Kudla, Rosenzweig, Szczyrba & Weissbach (2022), ICSMGE Sydney — publishes the full ~125-event population 2006-2018 in English through the ISSMGE open library.
Modern problem: Ghahramani, Nahyan, et al. (2020), "The use of LiDAR as a reference topography in Hpa-an and Mogok segments of the Sagaing Fault," and the tailings-mobility regression it is part of, states that flow-path confinement and tailings type visibly affect mobility "however, the data are not stratified enough to incorporate these factors into the regression analysis yet" at n = 33, and closes with "currently building the database and investigating the effects of other attributes of the tailings and downstream topography." Zero co-occurrence of the Lusatian corpus (Lusatia / Setzungsfliessen / Kudla / Weissbach / Wittig) with the tailings-flow-mobility literature per three independent searches.
Cheapest next check: ~2-3 days of one geotechnical engineer's time, no cost. Step 1: assemble every documented loose-saturated-sand static liquefaction with a published PRE-failure phreatic surface and toe/crest geometry — plausible set is Nerlerk berm, Wachusett North Dike, Calaveras, Fort Peck, Jupia, Merriespruit, Sullivan, Mount Polley perimeter embankment, Cadia NTSF, Fundao (n ~8-12). Extract h_F and h_K; compute h_F/h_K and compare against 0.333 for a measured or assumed cap friction angle. Score flow-vs-no-significant-horizontal-movement against (a) the Wittig threshold and (b) Ghahramani's confined/unconfined binary by simple 2x2 tables, reported as descriptive screens. Step 2 (parallel, 2-3 weeks, ~€15 ILL): obtain Boettge, Loebel, Wiesner & Wittig 2018 (qucosa:23248) and Weissbach 2020 Anhang 3, and request the 2024 LBGR Brandenburg volume (Grosser & Szczyrba); if that already makes the tailings link the novelty claim collapses. Step 3 only if 1 and 2 survive: ask LMBV/BIUG for the per-event table behind Weissbach & Kudla 2014 for out-of-sample retrodiction.

Author, affiliation, venue, the h_F/h_K > 0.333 criterion at phi = 30 degrees, the 0.394 value at FOS 1.4, the explicit statement that unit weight and slope inclination drop out, the 67-event base, the 5/43/19 category partition, the measurement-accuracy caveat, the under-recording admission for category 3, the "sehr gut" end-contour agreement and the 1.7/1.9-degree worked cases are all present verbatim. Both Ghahramani quotes and n = 33 were separately confirmed from NHESS 20:3425. Headline: Banks (CSIRO, 1978) defined an "optimal standard of sealing" for controlled-atmosphere grain storage as a whole-container fractional gas interchange rate (pressure-decay half-life on the filled container, <5 %/day for 300-10,000 t stores) because wind-driven loss should be reduced only until it is negligible against thermally driven headspace loss; the modern hermetic-bag field has standardised on a liner material rating (OTR in cc/m2/day, ASABE X657 draft), which carries no information about container geometry, seam quality or temperature swing, and no acceptance test for airtightness exists for a 20-100 kg bag.
Old source: Banks, H. J. (1978), "Recent Advances in the Use of Modified Atmospheres for Stored Product Pest Control," Proc. 2nd Int. Working Conf. Stored-Product Entomology, Ibadan, Nigeria, Sep 1978, pp. ~96-105 (sealing section pp. 99-100). https://hortscans.ces.ncsu.edu/uploads/p/r/proceedi_51a6283e2de55.pdf — sealing criterion stated verbatim; <5 %/day for 300-10000 t stores, <20 m3/hr at 250 Pa for ISO freight containers; Table II pressure-decay times on filled bins (Bordertown I 100 s, Bordertown II 1600 s, Harden 13,600 t 470 s on a 125-62.5 Pa decay). The underlying derivation is Banks, H. J., and Annis, P. C. (1977), "Suggested procedures for controlled atmosphere storage of dry grain," CSIRO Division of Entomology Technical Paper No. 13, 23 pp — grey literature, no digital copy located, remains unread.
Modern problem: Williams, S. B., Murdock, L. L., Kharel, K., and Baributsa, D. (2016), "Grain size and grain depth matter in the effort to kill insects in hermetically-stored commodities," J. Stored Products Research 69, 65-71 — accounts for leakage as a single 1.5 mm hole plus grain-bulk diffusion resistance, in 4 cm PVC pipes at a deliberately constant 26 C and 30% RH ("we limited the influence of temperature and moisture from our trials"), with no Banks/Annis/CSIRO/pressure-decay citation in a ~40-reference list. ASABE X657 draft is a gas-barrier-liner material standard (OTR per ASTM D3985/F1927), no whole-container acceptance test. Pressure-decay has been applied to silo bags, cocoons and permanent silos; no published filled-bag half-life acceptance threshold calibrated to the 2% insect-lethal O2 level exists for a 20-100 kg hermetic bag.
Cheapest next check: ~$2,000-2,500 and 12-14 weeks (one technician-month) in consumables. Buy 36 commercial 50 kg hermetic bags across three liner OTR classes (12 each of ~20 um HDPE, ~50 um multilayer, ~80 um EVOH). Fill with maize at ~13% MC (~1.8 t). On each bag measure (a) pressure-decay half-life from 250 to 125 Pa with a $40 digital manometer and hand bulb pump, repeated at two fill levels (90% and 70%) so envelope compliance separates from leakage by regression, and (b) headspace O2 against the 2 % insect threshold with galvanic cells. Run six bags per class outdoors under real diurnal swing and six indoors at constant temperature, 90 days. Test: does initial filled-bag pressure-decay half-life predict time-to-5%-O2 and 90-day O2 integral better than vendor liner OTR, and does the indoor/outdoor contrast show the thermal term is non-negligible at bag scale (which would falsify the lead's own stated rationale while supporting its metric)? Independently, request CSIRO Technical Paper No. 13 (1977) by ILL from CSIRO's Black Mountain library (~$20, 2 weeks) — the single highest-value cheap move.
Verifier notes: Upstream verifier 1 (score 7) downloaded the Ibadan proceedings PDF, extracted text with pdftotext, and verified every quoted phrase verbatim including the author line, the optimal-sealing criterion, the <5 %/day figure scoped to 300-10,000 tonnes, the <20 m3/hr at 250 Pa container standard, the 1978 complaint that pressure tests are "seldom given," Table II's decay times, and reference (2) to Banks & Annis TP 13. The modern counterpart (Williams et al. 2016) was fetched from the publisher PDF and the "limited the influence of temperature and moisture from our trials" quote confirmed; a grep for Banks/Annis/CSIRO/pressure decay/air exchange/leakage rate in that paper's full text returned zero hits. Caveats, carried as the upstream verifiers raised them: 1. **Banks himself excludes hermetic and pit storage from the sealed-storage engineering review in its first paragraph.** He drew the exact boundary this lead proposes to cross — which is both the undercut and the mechanism for the gap. The <5 %/day number is scoped to 300-10,000 t storages; it is a method, not a number to carry across. 2. **The lead's stated rationale is partly wrong physics.** The breathing volume in a filled bag is interstitial void air (~25-30 L in a 50 kg bag at 40% porosity), not headspace, and a thin bag tracks nearly the full diurnal swing while a 10,000 t bulk is thermally buffered. Thermal fractional interchange (dT/T ~ 5% per cycle) does not "almost vanish" at bag scale and may exceed the silo case. The surviving part of the claim is the area/volume term (~75-100x bag-vs-silo), which does hold. The experimental design above (indoor/outdoor contrast, two fill levels) is intended to measure the thermal term rather than argue around it. 3. **Envelope compliance can confound pressure-decay on a floppy liner.** A floppy liner is compliant, so a 250 Pa decay half-life on a 50 kg bag conflates compliance with leakage; Banks tested rigid filled bins. The two-fill-level regression above separates these. 4. **The actual derivation lives in CSIRO Technical Paper No. 13 (1977), 23 pp, which no verifier obtained.** The scaling argument rests on an unread paper; ILL request is the first move. 5. **Pre-emption is partial.** Carpaneto et al. 2016 already apply pressure-decay testing to field plastic grain bags; the novelty here reduces to a size extension plus a biologically calibrated threshold. 6. **Vocabulary split is not as clean as first framed.** The packaging world already owns whole-package leak tests (ASTM F2095 pressure decay with restraining plates, F1140, F2338), including documented handling of film-stretch and volume-sensitivity confounds. The ISU NC-213 model couples OTR to a whole-bag O2 balance. 7. **The upstream refuting verifier (score 2)** argued the Banks criterion is used with the wrong sign (Banks's optimum marks where extra sealing is wasted; the hermetic-bag field already tolerates leaky containers because insect respiration dominates O2 depletion), and that the 2-5 % O2 target is not scale-free (lethality runs through desiccation and depends on infestation, temperature and moisture; 8% gives no complete mortality per Ranabhat/Maier Insects 2023). Any proposal should quote <2 % as the biologically meaningful threshold rather than 2-5 %. Upstream score 7/5/2 (one refuted) on 2026-10-21; destination undecided. Found by an automated literature sweep; not refereed. A hypothesis worth one cheap check, not a finding.

Headline: A 1960s guanidine-containing polyketide macrolide (azalomycin F) was documented to kill C. albicans by membrane permeabilization; it has apparently never been tested against C. auris or the C. haemulonii complex.
Old source: Sugawara et al. (1968), "Chemistry of azalomycin F", J. Antibiot. 21:83, doi 10.7164/antibiotics.21.83. Supporting 1967/1969/1973 papers and Miyake 1990 all exist and were located by the source verifiers.
Modern problem: 2022 review of guanidine antifungals (discusses C. auris at length but contains no macrolides) and a 2019 review of ~48 guanidine-containing polyhydroxyl macrolides (tabulates Candida work only for albicans and classic non-albicans species, never C. auris). Two adjacent literatures with no bridge; zero co-occurrence hits for the pair.
Cheapest next check: One CLSI M27 broth microdilution plate against a ~20-isolate C. auris panel spanning clades I-V and including azole/amphotericin-B/echinocandin-resistant isolates. Approx. 1 week, a few hundred USD, any clinical mycology lab.
Verifier notes: The upstream verifier confirmed the Sugawara 1968 paper says what the scout claimed about membrane permeabilization and leakage of cell constituents in C. albicans, and located the supporting mid-century papers. The gap between the two modern reviews is real and was reproduced in search: a 2019 review of guanidine-containing polyhydroxyl macrolides tabulates Candida work for albicans and the classic non-albicans species only, and a 2022 review of guanidine antifungals discusses C. auris at length but contains no macrolides. No study pairs azalomycin F (or its congeners) with C. auris or the C. haemulonii complex. Caveats to carry forward: - Membrane-permeabilizing polyenes already treat C. auris (amphotericin B); the hypothesis is only interesting if azalomycin F has activity against amphotericin-B-resistant isolates, so the test panel must include them. - Mid-century MICs on C. albicans do not automatically transfer to a different species in a different decade; "never tested" is a cheap-check argument, not a prediction of activity. - Azalomycin F is a mixture of congeners historically; sourcing a reasonably pure preparation is part of the cost. Found by an automated literature sweep; not refereed. A hypothesis worth one cheap check, not a finding. Nothing here is medical or clinical advice.

Headline: Pyrrolnitrin (from Pseudomonas aureofaciens, 1964) was abandoned as a systemic antifungal because of ~90% loss of activity in serum, but its documented in vitro potency and the TOPICAL / SURFACE sites where C. auris actually has to be killed (colonised skin and dry hospital surfaces) sidestep that specific failure mode.
Old source: Gordee RS, Matthews TR (1969), "Systemic antifungal activity of pyrrolnitrin", Appl Microbiol 17(5):690-694, PMC377781. Mechanism: Tripathi & Gottlieb (upstream respiratory block, before ubiquinone).
Modern problem: No susceptibility data for pyrrolnitrin, or its photostable commercial analogues fludioxonil and fenpiclonil, against C. auris or the C. haemulonii complex (checked Europe PMC, OpenAlex, Google Scholar and patents). The modern C. auris surface/skin decontamination problem is well established; the connection to this old antifungal class is not made.
Cheapest next check: Standard CLSI/EUCAST broth microdilution against a C. auris isolate panel (plus a parallel surface time-kill assay for the surface-decontamination arm), using pyrrolnitrin (Cayman 35099, CAS 1018-71-9) and fludioxonil as catalogue reagents. ~3 days, under USD 400 for a lab with a hood and plate reader.
Verifier notes: Verifiers in the upstream ledger fetched both primary sources (Gordee & Matthews 1969 and the Tripathi & Gottlieb mechanism paper). Confirmed: in vitro activity range 0.78-100 ug/mL across the organisms tested, ~90% loss of activity in serum, and a conclusion that is explicitly scoped to SYSTEMIC use. The 1969 paper itself notes prior efficacy against superficial infections, so the source actually signposts the topical pivot rather than contradicting it. Co-occurrence check performed: zero susceptibility data for pyrrolnitrin or its photostable commercial analogues (fludioxonil / fenpiclonil, used as agricultural fungicides) against C. auris or the C. haemulonii complex, across Europe PMC, OpenAlex, Scholar and patents. Mechanism holds against the obvious expert objection: the respiratory block pyrrolnitrin imposes sits UPSTREAM of ubiquinone, so Candida's alternative oxidase pathway does not bypass it. All three source-side verifiers voted survived (scores 6, 5, and one on a broken scale per the upstream runlog). A relevant note from the source ledger: a prior scout rejected pyrrolnitrin at a low score; it returned here with a different framing (topical/surface rather than systemic) and survived. Rejections in this routine are not permanently dead when a different angle genuinely addresses the earlier objection. Caveats: - Fludioxonil's known mode of action in filamentous fungi is HOG-pathway activation, not the same respiratory block; the two analogues are not interchangeable for the mechanistic claim. - Agricultural resistance to fludioxonil exists in some phytopathogens; cross-resistance in Candida is not established either way. - "Topical/surface" is a use-case claim, not a demonstration of efficacy or safety on human skin; this lead is about the in vitro gap, not clinical use. Found by an automated literature sweep; not refereed. A hypothesis worth one cheap check, not a finding. Nothing here is medical or clinical advice.

Headline: Change the ANION, not the pH — substitute potassium sulphate (K2SO4) for muriate of potash (KCl) in established cacao, and treat soil-solution chloride as a controllable driver of bean cadmium via CdCl+ / CdCl2(aq) complexation; a 1994 Tasmanian potato field series shows 20-30% lower tuber and petiole Cd under K2SO4 at 4 of 6 sites.
Old source: Sparrow LA, Johnstone PR, Salardini AA (1994), "Cadmium and zinc in potato tubers and petioles as affected by potassium fertilisers", Aust. J. Agric. Res. 45(1):243-249, doi 10.1071/AR9940243. Companion: Sparrow, Salardini & Bishop (1993), AJAR 44:845-853 (broadcast lime did not change tuber Cd at any site across pH 5.2-7.1 on high-OM Fe-oxide-rich krasnozems).
Modern problem: PNS BAFS 421:2025 (national adoption of Codex CXC 81-2022, the code of practice for reducing Cd in cacao beans) — full-text extracted by a source verifier, zero hits for chloride, potash, KCl or potassium in any form; fertiliser clauses name only lime/dolomite, organic fertilisers, MgSO4, CaSO4, ZnSO4, zeolite, biochar, vinasse and apatite. The Alliance Bioversity-CIAT / NICOLE cacao-Cd mitigation report (232k characters) likewise contains no discussion of K source or Cd-chloro complexation.
Cheapest next check: Retrospective reanalysis of existing georeferenced LAC cacao-Cd survey cohorts (Clima-LoCa / Alliance Bioversity-CIAT / Peruvian INIA / Ecuador orchard survey), which already hold bean Cd, soil Cd, pH and %OC for hundreds of farms. Add K-product (MOP vs SOP vs KNO3 vs none) and irrigation-water source from farm records, run water-soluble Cl- and SO4(2-) by IC on archived extracts, and regress bean Cd on K source and Cl- with soil Cd, pH and OC as covariates. USD 2-25k, 2 weeks to 3 months. Decision rule: if the Cl- term adds no explanatory power over pH and extractable Cd, the lead dies before anyone funds a plantation trial.
Verifier notes: All three source-side verifiers independently fetched Sparrow et al. 1994 and confirmed the paraphrase sentence by sentence: six matched-rate Russet Burbank field experiments, banded DAP plus either K2SO4 or KCl; at 4 of 6 sites tuber AND petiole Cd were 20-30% lower under K2SO4; the authors call it of "considerable promise". The companion 1993 paper's null result on broadcast lime across pH 5.2-7.1 on high-OM krasnozems is a direct warning for high-OM cacao soils, where lime trials have been slow and inconsistent. The cacao-side omission was checked against the AUTHORITATIVE documents (PNS BAFS 421:2025 and the Alliance Bioversity-CIAT / NICOLE mitigation report), not asserted. A Colombian greenhouse study reports a soil-K / foliar-Cd correlation (r2 = -0.56) with no reference to the accompanying anion — the field has the data but not the concept. Caveats raised in the source ledger, all preserved verbatim: 1. **Not novel as a concept, only as a transfer.** CSIRO's own potato grower brochure and an Australian fertiliser-industry agritopic already advise sulphate over muriate of potash to manage Cd. The novelty is strictly that nobody has run it in cacao. 2. **Effect size is 20-30%, below the 30-60% the problem needs**, and it is a tuber/petiole result, not a seed result. 3. **The sulphate half of the mechanism is weaker than the chloride half, and the scout conflated them.** Wang et al. 2019 found K2SO4 slightly INCREASED Cd in wheat and pak choi and reduced it substantially only in rice, where sulphate reduction to sulphide and CdS precipitation operates — a mechanism that cannot run in aerobic cacao soil. Hussain et al. 2022 found sulphate had no significant field effect on rice grain Cd. The aerobic prior rests essentially on the one 1994 potato series. 4. **The failure mode predicts attenuation in the target environment.** Sparrow's two null sites were attributed to leaching and background irrigation chloride. LAC cacao sits in 1800-3000 mm/yr humid tropics where chloride is the most leachable anion, so fertiliser Cl may be a transient pulse rather than a standing condition. Read the other way, this says the effect appears only where fertiliser Cl dominates the Cl budget. **This is the single biggest hole.** 5. Much LAC cacao is low-input; on many exceeding farms there is no KCl to substitute. K2SO4 also costs well above KCl per unit K at cacao K rates of 118-176 kg K/ha, so "no cost increase of consequence" is unsupported. 6. No chlorine requirement or Cl toxicity threshold for Theobroma cacao was located; the agronomic-risk claim is unevaluated. DESTINATION in the source ledger is undecided. The natural recipients would be the cacao-Cd programmes named above; nothing has been drafted or sent. Found by an automated literature sweep; not refereed. A hypothesis worth one cheap check, not a finding. Nothing here is agronomic, regulatory or financial advice.

Headline: Calcium phosphate (apatite / amorphous calcium phosphate) has apparently never been tested as an atmospheric ice-nucleating phase, although the insect-cryobiology literature names insoluble calcium-phosphate crystalloid deposits as a distinct class of endogenous ice nucleators; apatite is a real accessory component of soil and desert dust, bone and guano dust, and phosphate-fertilizer and phosphogypsum dust.
Old source: Lee RE, Costanzo JP, Mugnano JA (1996), "Regulation of supercooling and ice nucleation in insects", Eur J Entomol 93(3):405-418. https://www.eje.cz/artkey/eje-199603-0011_Regulation_of_supercooling_and_ice_nucleation_in_insects.php — abstract and body state that insoluble crystalloid deposits such as calcium phosphate, present in a variety of insects, represent a newly discovered class of endogenous ice nucleators. Primary measurement: Mugnano, Lee & Taylor (1996), calcium-phosphate spherules raised crystallization T in 10 uL droplets from -18.4 to -10.1 C.
Modern problem: Kaufmann et al. (2016), "Ice nucleation efficiency of natural dust samples in the immersion mode", Atmos. Chem. Phys. 16:11177 — reference-mineral immersion-freezing survey; mineral list is quartz, calcite, clays, K-feldspars, (Na,Ca)-feldspars, microcline, dolomite, muscovite, dolostone and Arizona test dust; no phosphate of any kind. Four further searches returned zero studies measuring the ice-nucleating ability of any phosphate mineral. A 2026 ACP perthite-feldspar paper notes small apatite inclusions in a tested feldspar sample and does not test them.
Cheapest next check: Standard microlitre droplet-freezing cold-stage assay (FINC / NIPI / Micro-PINGUIN style, 96 x 1 uL) on synthetic hydroxyapatite, synthetic fluorapatite and a geological standard such as Durango apatite — each ball-milled and BET-characterised — at 0.1 and 1.0 wt%, with microcline as positive control and milled quartz as negative. Report n_s(T). Roughly USD 1-3k and 2-3 days of bench time for any group that already owns a cold stage. A null result kills the lead immediately.
Verifier notes: The upstream source ledger notes this was the one lead in that batch to reach the "worth one cheap check" threshold, and only just (scores 6 / 5 / 2; the third verifier voted refuted). A source verifier fetched Lee, Costanzo & Mugnano 1996 verbatim and confirmed the quoted claim about calcium-phosphate crystalloid deposits as a distinct class of endogenous ice nucleators. A verifier also fetched Kaufmann et al. 2016 and confirmed the mineral list contains no phosphate. Caveats, all preserved from the source ledger: 1. **Partial prior art, and it is real.** Cornwell et al. 2024 (JGR-Atmospheres, SGP site) found PO2- and PO3- signals significantly enriched in ice-crystal residuals versus ambient particles by single-particle mass spectrometry. The atmospheric phosphate-INP link is therefore not untouched; what is untouched is the laboratory measurement. 2. **The numbers are weak.** The primary Mugnano/Lee/Taylor measurement is in 10 uL droplets, raising crystallization T from -18.4 to -10.1 C. Rescaled to micron particles in picolitre cloud droplets, that warm-onset claim weakens considerably. One verifier marked the lead refuted on this basis. 3. **Abundance.** Apatite is typically well under 1 wt% of soil and desert dust, so even microcline-like per-area activity would make a minor global contribution. The bridge is strongest for localised sources (fertilizer, phosphogypsum, bone and guano dust), not the global INP reservoir. 4. **Relevance is partly self-undercutting.** The scout framed this against the Southern Ocean shortwave bias, but the Southern Ocean is the most dust-poor region on Earth. A new continental-dust accessory mineral speaks to the Arctic / continental half of the problem at best. 5. The 1996 source gives no nucleation temperature, no surface-area normalisation, and no proof that the deposit rather than an associated protein is the active phase. What survives the caveats is a cheap, falsifiable laboratory measurement that nobody has made on reference apatite samples. If positive, the natural home is addition to community INP parameterization datasets; if null, the lead dies for the cost of a few days of cold-stage time. Found by an automated literature sweep; not refereed. A hypothesis worth one cheap check, not a finding.
